_comment: Comparative knowledge for the Perazim Guide's drift detection. Status DRAFT_PENDING_LEVI: every entry is a summary written for review, not an approved source. Only the text in 'summary', 'origin' and 'scripture' is shown to the model. 'internal_note' is never shown to the model or to users. Scripture references are KJV and are retrieved verbatim from the bundled KJV database; no other translation is quoted. Entries are context only: the model may explain them but may not cite them. Standard: historic Protestant, Evangelical and Pentecostal orthodoxy, with Scripture as supreme authority. Under Levi's ruling O-2 the guide does not describe the Roman Catholic or Eastern Orthodox churches; their teachings appear here only so drift can be detected and answered from Scripture.

entries.summary: Karma is the teaching, held in Hindu, Buddhist and Jain thought, that a person's intentional actions bring results that shape later experience, including a later life.
entries.origin: Karma comes from Hindu, Buddhist and Jain teaching. It is tied to reincarnation and to the goal of escaping the cycle of rebirth.
entries.scripture: The Bible does not teach karma. It teaches that people die once and then face judgment (Hebrews 9:27). Salvation is a gift of grace through faith, not the balance of good and bad deeds (Ephesians 2:8-9). Galatians 6:7 warns that people reap what they sow, but it speaks of a life lived for the flesh or the Spirit in this life, not of a cycle of rebirth.

entries.summary: Reincarnation, or rebirth, is the teaching that a soul or stream of consciousness passes through many lives in different bodies, shaped by karma, until liberation.
entries.origin: Reincarnation is central to Hindu, Buddhist and Jain teaching, and it is also found in some New Age and esoteric writing.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that each person lives once, dies once, and then faces judgment (Hebrews 9:27). Jesus's words to the thief, 'To day shalt thou be with me in paradise' (Luke 23:43), and Paul's desire 'to depart, and to be with Christ' (Philippians 1:23) describe life after death with Christ, not a return to earth. Reincarnation is therefore not compatible with the biblical view.

sources.title: Upanishads (Max Müller translation, Sacred Books of the East)

entries.summary: Nirvana (Buddhism) and moksha (Hinduism) are the goal of release from suffering or from the cycle of rebirth, understood differently in each tradition.
entries.origin: These are goals of Buddhist and Hindu practice. Buddhism speaks of the end of craving, and Hinduism of liberation of the self.
entries.scripture: Scripture does not describe release from rebirth. It offers eternal life as a gift of God through Jesus Christ (John 3:16) and the hope of being with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Liberation in Scripture comes through the Son, not through self-effort: 'If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed' (John 8:36).

sources.title: Pali Canon (Rhys Davids and Oldenberg translations, Sacred Books of the Buddhists)

entries.summary: Purgatory is a teaching of a temporary state of purification after death for those who die in grace but still need cleansing before heaven.
entries.origin: Purgatory is a teaching from later church tradition. It is not found in Scripture and is not part of the Protestant or Evangelical understanding of the afterlife.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that the blood of Christ cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7) and that believers are justified freely by grace through faith (Romans 3:24). Paul says that to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Nothing in Scripture adds a further cleansing after death. Christians should judge what they believe by the Bible, and the state after death is a matter of God's word alone.
entries.internal_note: Catholic teaching (Catechism 1030-1032). Use for drift only. Never name the source church.

sources.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraphs 1030-1032 (paragraph reference only; the text is not reproduced)

entries.summary: The teaching that the saints and Mary can be asked to pray for the living, and that prayers can be addressed to them, is found in later Christian tradition.
entries.origin: Asking the saints or Mary to intercede is a teaching from later church tradition, not from the New Testament.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches one mediator between God and people: 'For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus' (1 Timothy 2:5). Believers are invited to come to God directly through him (Hebrews 4:16). Prayer is addressed to God the Father, in the name of Jesus (John 14:13). The Bible also forbids the worship of anything made by hand that takes God's place (Exodus 20:4-5).
entries.internal_note: Catholic and Orthodox practice (Catechism 2683, prayer to saints). Use for drift only. Never name the source church.

sources.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph 2683 (paragraph reference only)

entries.summary: Titles such as co-redeemer, mediatrix or queen of heaven, given to Mary, are teachings from later tradition that go beyond what Scripture says about her.
entries.origin: Titles for Mary as co-redeemer, mediatrix or queen of heaven developed in later tradition. Scripture calls Mary blessed among women and the mother of Jesus, and she points to her Son (John 2:5).
entries.scripture: Scripture names Jesus as the only mediator (1 Timothy 2:5) and the one Saviour who saves by his own work (Acts 4:12). Mary herself says that God is her Saviour (Luke 1:47). Redemption is finished in Christ, and no one shares his office.
entries.internal_note: Catholic teaching on Mary and the Assumption. Use for drift only. Never name the source church.

sources.title: Scripture and public-domain commentary summaries (Easton, Smith dictionaries)

entries.summary: The use of icons, statues, rosaries and prayer beads as aids to prayer and devotion, with bowing or kissing them, comes from later tradition.
entries.origin: Icons and rosaries developed in later church tradition. Protestant and Evangelical Christians hold that the second commandment forbids making and bowing to images used in worship.
entries.scripture: The second commandment says: 'Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image... thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them' (Exodus 20:4-5). Jesus said that true worshippers worship God in spirit and in truth (John 4:23-24), not through images.
entries.internal_note: Catholic and Orthodox veneration of icons and images. Use for drift only. Never name the source church.

entries.summary: Soul sleep is the teaching, held by some Adventist and Christadelphian groups, that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection.
entries.origin: Soul sleep is taught by some Seventh-day Adventist and Christadelphian writers. Most Christians hold that the believer is with the Lord at death.
entries.scripture: Jesus told the thief, 'To day shalt thou be with me in paradise' (Luke 23:43), and Paul said he would rather be absent from the body and present with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Scripture also speaks of the rich man and Lazarus, both conscious after death (Luke 16:19-31). The resurrection of the body is a future hope, not the start of conscious life.

sources.title: Seventh-day Adventist Church Fundamental Beliefs (summary only)

entries.summary: Conditional immortality is the teaching that the soul is not inherently immortal, that only those who receive eternal life live on, and that the wicked are finally destroyed rather than suffer forever.
entries.origin: Conditional immortality is taught by some Jehovah's Witness, Seventh-day Adventist and Christadelphian writers.
entries.scripture: Scripture says that the wicked will be punished with everlasting punishment (Matthew 25:46) and that the lake of fire is for the devil, the beast and the false prophet, who will be tormented day and night for ever (Revelation 20:10). Eternal life is a gift of God in Christ (Romans 6:23), and the soul that sins is accountable to God (Ezekiel 18:4).

entries.summary: All-paths teaching holds that all religions lead to the same God or the same end, so that the exclusive claims of Jesus are set aside.
entries.origin: The all-paths view is common in modern pluralism and in some New Age and Hindu-influenced writing.
entries.scripture: Jesus said, 'I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me' (John 14:6). Peter said there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). The Bible does not present many roads to God. It presents one way, through Christ.

entries.summary: The teaching that the self is identical with God or the ultimate reality, as in Hindu Advaita (atman is Brahman) and some New Age writing, that you are God or divine by nature.
entries.origin: Atman is Brahman comes from Upanishadic Hindu thought. The idea that everyone is God is found in some New Age and mystical writing.
entries.scripture: Scripture says that God created people in his image (Genesis 1:27) and that the Creator is distinct from creation (Isaiah 40:25; Romans 1:25). Humans are not God. Jesus is the only Son who is God by nature (John 1:1; Colossians 2:9), and believers are adopted as children of God by grace (Galatians 4:5).

entries.summary: Eternal progression is the Latter-day Saint teaching that God was once a man, that people can progress to become gods, and that exaltation is reached through works and temple ordinances.
entries.origin: This teaching comes from Latter-day Saint sources, including the Doctrine and Covenants and later sermons of Joseph Smith and his successors.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that God is not a man (Numbers 23:19) and that there is one God, with none formed before or after him (Isaiah 43:10). Believers are called children of God and heirs with Christ (Romans 8:16-17), not gods in the making. Eternal life is the free gift of God through Jesus Christ (Romans 6:23).

sources.title: Doctrine and Covenants and Book of Mormon (1830 text is public domain; current texts are copyright)

entries.summary: Salvation by works is the teaching that people are saved or kept saved by their deeds, or by grace together with what they do, as in the phrase 'after all we can do' from the Book of Mormon.
entries.origin: Salvation by works is a teaching of some Latter-day Saint, Jehovah's Witness and other groups, and of many world religions that weigh deeds.
entries.scripture: Scripture says: 'For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast' (Ephesians 2:8-9). Paul says righteousness comes through faith in Christ, not through the law (Romans 3:20-28). Good works are the fruit of salvation, not its price.

sources.title: Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 25:23 (1830 edition is public domain; verify the wording against the 1830 text before quoting)

entries.summary: In many African traditional religions, ancestors are the departed who remain part of the family and community. Some communities honour them, ask them for help, or offer to them, while also recognising a Supreme God above them.
entries.origin: Ancestor veneration is a practice in many African traditional religions, including Kikuyu, Luo, Akan and Luganda communities. Practices vary widely between communities and families.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that people should honour their parents (Exodus 20:12) and remember the faithful dead with thanks, but that the dead cannot be asked for help or made mediators (Deuteronomy 18:10-12). Believers are told that God alone is the one to whom prayer is addressed, and that there is one mediator, Christ (1 Timothy 2:5). Christians can honour family members without seeking their intercession.

sources.title: Mbiti, African Religions and Philosophy (1969), summary only

entries.summary: Groups that deny the Trinity hold that God is one person who appears in different modes (Oneness, or modalism), or that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are separate beings or gods (Jehovah's Witnesses and some Latter-day Saint writing).
entries.origin: Oneness Pentecostal, modalist, Jehovah's Witness and some Latter-day Saint teaching deny the Trinity. Historic Christian orthodoxy, including Protestant, Evangelical and Pentecostal churches, affirms one God in three persons.
entries.scripture: Scripture says: 'Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD' (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Father, Son and Holy Spirit are named together in the baptismal commission (Matthew 28:19). The Son is God (John 1:1; Hebrews 1:8), and the Holy Spirit is a person who teaches, grieves and speaks (John 14:26; Acts 13:2). The Father is not the Son (John 14:28).

entries.summary: Jehovah's Witness teaching holds that Jesus is a created being, the archangel Michael, and not God the Son who is eternal.
entries.origin: This teaching is specific to Jehovah's Witness publications and differs from Scripture and historic Christian belief.
entries.scripture: Scripture says that Jesus is the eternal Word who was God (John 1:1-3), that all things were created by him (Colossians 1:16), and that he is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15). The angels are commanded to worship him (Hebrews 1:6). Michael is an angel who is not the Son of God (Jude 9).

entries.summary: Some groups teach that the Holy Spirit is an impersonal active force or power of God, not a divine person.
entries.origin: This is the teaching of Jehovah's Witness publications, and it differs from historic Christian and Pentecostal belief.
entries.scripture: Scripture names the Holy Spirit as a person who teaches (John 14:26), speaks (Acts 13:2), can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30), and can be lied to (Acts 5:3-4). He is called God (Acts 5:3-4). The Holy Spirit is also one of the three persons named in the baptismal commission (Matthew 28:19).

entries.summary: Baptism for the dead is a Latter-day Saint practice of being baptised by proxy for people who have died, so they can accept the gospel in the afterlife.
entries.origin: Baptism for the dead is a practice of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that people believe and are baptised in this life, as a response to the gospel (Mark 16:16; Acts 2:38). The passage in 1 Corinthians 15:29 that some use for proxy baptism is a difficult text that Protestant and Evangelical commentators read in many ways. It does not establish a practice of proxy baptism, and the rest of Scripture ties salvation to faith in this life (Hebrews 9:27).

entries.summary: Some groups, including Seventh-day Adventists, teach that the Sabbath must be kept on Saturday as a binding command for Christians, and that Sunday observance is a mark of error.
entries.origin: Saturday Sabbath keeping is the teaching of Seventh-day Adventist and some other groups. Most Christians worship on the first day of the week, the day of the resurrection.
entries.scripture: Scripture says: 'Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days' (Colossians 2:16). Believers are free in Christ, and Paul says that each should be fully persuaded in their own mind (Romans 14:5). Christ is Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28), and the first day is when the Lord rose from the dead (Mark 16:2).

sources.title: Seventh-day Adventist Church Fundamental Beliefs (summary only)

entries.summary: New Age teaching often speaks of universal energy, the law of attraction, chakras, a higher self, or manifesting reality by focused thought, and treats the self as the source of healing and destiny.
entries.origin: These ideas come from New Age, Theosophical and occult writing, mixed with ideas from Hindu and Buddhist thought.
entries.scripture: Scripture teaches that God is a personal Spirit who created the world and is not an energy field (John 4:24). Healing and destiny come from God's will and grace, not from manifesting or from inner energy (James 5:14-15). Believers are told to test every spirit (1 John 4:1) and to avoid divination and occult practice (Deuteronomy 18:10-12).

entries.summary: Christian Science teaches that God is Mind, that matter and sickness are illusions or errors, and that healing comes through understanding this, not through medicine or the physical death and resurrection of Jesus.
entries.origin: Christian Science was founded by Mary Baker Eddy, whose book Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures (1875) is its main text.
entries.scripture: Scripture describes Jesus as a real man who was born, suffered, died, and rose bodily (Luke 24:39; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). It also describes real sickness and healing through God's power and through prayer (James 5:14-16). The atonement is by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 1:7), not by a change in understanding alone.

sources.title: Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures (1875, public domain)

entries.summary: Secular worldviews hold that there is no God, that science alone gives knowledge, and that morality is only human custom or preference.
entries.origin: Secular humanism, scientific naturalism and moral relativism are the main forms of this worldview.
entries.scripture: Scripture says that the heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1) and that the fool has said in his heart, there is no God (Psalm 14:1). Moral law is written on human hearts (Romans 2:14-15), and the Bible speaks of a just judge to whom everyone is accountable (Romans 14:12). Faith and reason are not opposed, and science and Scripture are both gifts that can be studied with care.

entries.summary: Islamic teaching holds that Jesus was not crucified and that someone else was made to appear to be him, while Jesus was taken up by God.
entries.origin: This is the teaching of the Qur'an (Surah 4:157) and Islamic tradition. The Qur'an is not quoted here: the guide describes this teaching in its own words.
entries.scripture: The Bible reports that Jesus was crucified and died (Matthew 27:50; Acts 2:23), and that he rose from the dead (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Paul says the gospel is 'Christ crucified' (1 Corinthians 1:23). The death and resurrection of Jesus are central to the Christian faith, and the claim that he was not crucified is not supported by the historical witness of the New Testament.

sources.title: Qur'an (not quoted; paraphrase only under Levi's ruling O-1)

entries.summary: Islamic teaching holds that God has no son, that Jesus is a prophet and messenger of God and not divine, and that the Christian teaching of the Trinity is a mistake.
entries.origin: This is the teaching of Islam, including the Qur'an. The Qur'an is not quoted here: the guide describes this teaching in its own words.
entries.scripture: Scripture says that Jesus is the eternal Son of God (John 1:14; Hebrews 1:2-3), that he is God (John 1:1; Titus 2:13), and that he is the only mediator between God and people (1 Timothy 2:5). The Father sent the Son (John 3:16). Jesus said, 'I and my Father are one' (John 10:30).

sources.title: Qur'an (not quoted; paraphrase only under Levi's ruling O-1)

entries.summary: The Protestant and Evangelical Bible contains 66 books: 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New Testament. Some Bibles also include extra books, called deuterocanonical or apocryphal, such as Tobit, Judith, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach and Baruch, and additions to Esther and Daniel.
entries.origin: The 66-book canon is the Bible used by Protestants, Evangelicals and Pentecostals. Some Bibles from other traditions add the extra books listed above.
entries.scripture: Protestant and Evangelical Christians hold that the 66 books are the inspired Word of God. The extra books are read for history and edification but are not used to establish doctrine. Scripture warns against adding to or taking away from God's words (Deuteronomy 4:2; Revelation 22:18-19). Jesus and the apostles spoke of the Scriptures as the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms (Luke 24:44).

entries.summary: A question asks whether a church or group is true, saved or a cult. The guide does not describe or judge such churches as institutions, and it does not give a verdict on any person.
entries.origin: This is a policy entry, not a teaching. It applies to churches named in questions.
entries.scripture: Scripture is the standard for every teaching. The guide answers by saying what Scripture teaches on the subject the user asked about, and it leaves the judgment of any person's heart to God (1 Samuel 16:7; Romans 14:12). The user can read the Bible for themselves (Acts 17:11).

entries.summary: A question names a group such as Latter-day Saints, Jehovah's Witnesses, Seventh-day Adventists, Oneness Pentecostals or Christian Science. The guide describes that group's teaching accurately from its own sources and evaluates it against Scripture.
entries.origin: These groups are described in the entries on Latter-day Saint, Jehovah's Witness, Seventh-day Adventist, Oneness, Christian Science and Christadelphian teaching.
entries.scripture: The guide explains the group's teaching in plain words, names the passages each side relies on, and then shows what Scripture teaches (Acts 17:11). It gives no verdict on any member's salvation and treats every person with dignity.
